title: I’m cutting 40% of my game because I fucked up.
author: Kiko_Production
selftext:
Hi everyone! I'm a solo developer working on **City Paradise**, a cozy city builder with a bit of story and some rather unusual characters.

And I think I made a pretty big mistake.

When I first started the project, I wanted to combine two genres: a city builder and a dating sim. You'd build and manage your own little town, but you'd also get to know its managers, develop relationships with them, uncover their stories, and occasionally step away from city management to do something completely different.

It sounded like a fun combination. And for a while, I genuinely enjoyed building it.

I added an in-game phone with different apps, messages from characters, relationship progression, unlockable upgrades tied to those relationships, mini-games, and visual novel sequences. Some scenes had their own environments, animations, camera compositions, and multiple character expressions.

The idea was that every manager would feel like a proper character rather than just another button in the UI.

**And then the scope started getting ridiculous.**

The game is divided into five stars, each representing a new stage of your city's development. At the first star, I've only introduced **two out of seven planned managers**.

And somehow, I've already accumulated around **180 individual character-related images**.

That includes dialogue expressions, character poses, avatars, icons, illustrations for scenes, different compositions, and various other assets.

1. For two characters. At the very beginning of the game.

If I continued at roughly the same pace, I could end up with something approaching **900 separate images** by the time the game was finished.

For a solo developer making his first game, that's absolutely insane.

And here's the thing: **I'm not an artist.**

A lot of this artwork is AI-assisted. But that doesn't mean I can just generate an image and immediately put it into the game. Every asset still needs direction, iteration, corrections, consistency checks, editing, and integration. Sometimes getting a single shot to look right takes an absurd amount of time.

Then there's the actual implementation: dialogue logic, animations, transitions, timing, UI, mini-game mechanics, save states, and making sure everything works together.

And that's just one scene.

Multiply that by seven characters, five progression stages, and all their possible interactions, and suddenly you're spending an enormous amount of time on everything *except the actual city builder*.

That's when I realized something.

**I was slowly turning my city builder into a collection of separate games, and losing sight of the reason I started making it.**

So I've decided to make a pretty drastic change.

I'm cutting a huge chunk of the relationship systems and shifting City Paradise toward a more focused, cozy city-building experience.

The managers aren't disappearing. They'll still have personalities, appear in the city, introduce new mechanics, and occasionally get their own small story moments. I'll probably keep a few simple visual novel scenes, especially some of the ones I've already finished.

But I no longer want the player constantly jumping between building a city, answering messages, grinding relationship points, playing unrelated mini-games, and watching elaborate cutscenes just to unlock another upgrade.

Instead, I want to focus on **the city itself**.

More building variety, better progression, interesting upgrades, a stronger economy, a more pleasant atmosphere, and residents who actually feel like they're living there.

I'd love to make individual citizens more memorable, too. Give them names, little events, maybe relationships and families eventually. Let players pick favorites and follow what happens to them.

Something that makes you care about the little town you've built, rather than constantly pulling you away from it.

Of course, this decision comes with another headache.

A lot of things are interconnected. Removing the relationship system means rethinking how upgrades work, changing parts of the tutorial, redesigning some UI, revisiting the economy and progression, and rewriting parts of the story.

Even the in-game phone might need to go.

So yeah, I'm basically preparing for a pretty major overhaul of a game I've already spent a ridiculous amount of time building.

**But I think it's better to recognize this now than spend another year creating content for a system I'm no longer sure belongs in the game.**

There's also something I've learned about AI-assisted solo development.

AI tools are incredibly powerful. They've allowed me to experiment with things I probably wouldn't have attempted on my own, from art pipelines and character assets to UI, scripting, and entire gameplay systems.

But they don't magically solve scope.

In some ways, they can make it worse.

When you suddenly have the ability to create so many things, it's incredibly tempting to keep adding more. Another mechanic, another scene, another character, another system.

And because you're technically capable of making it, you start convincing yourself that you *should* make it.

But someone still has to decide what actually belongs in the game.

And when you're working alone, without another developer or artist to bounce ideas off, it's surprisingly easy to lose perspective. You spend so much time solving individual problems that you stop questioning whether those problems needed to exist in the first place.

I think that's what happened to me.

That said, I don't consider all that work completely wasted. I've learned a ton about development, AI-assisted art workflows, UI design, animation, and how to put different systems together. A lot of those techniques and assets will still be useful, either in City Paradise or in future projects.

And some of the stuff I made along the way is genuinely pretty cool. It just doesn't all need to be in this game.

For now, I'm taking a short break from City Paradise to clear my head. During that time, I'm going to experiment with a much smaller side project: a co-op horror game based on an idea I've been wanting to try. Maybe I'll share some footage if the prototype turns into something interesting.

**I'm not abandoning City Paradise.** I still love the project, its world, and its characters.

I just think it needs to become a smaller, more focused game before it can become a better one.

If you've ever had to cut a huge part of your own project, I'd genuinely love to hear how you handled it.

And if you're making your first game solo, maybe don't try to build a city builder, dating sim, visual novel, and mini-game collection all at once.

Apparently, that's a terrible idea.
